articles.title: Nations Championship - England 78-15 Japan: Will Joseph scores five tries in first cap since 2022 as hosts score 13
articles.summary: Will Joseph scored five tries on his first England appearance since 2022 as Steve Borthwick's side destroyed Japan 78-15 in Saturday's Nations Championship.
articles.body:
Will Joseph (five), Freddie Steward, Ellis Genge, Cadan Murley, Ben Earl, George Martin, Ben Curry, Marcus Smith, Greg Fisilau score tries as England post huge Nations Championship victory, with Eddie Jones' Japan alarmingly inferior in contest; Joseph on first appearance since July 2022

By Michael Cantillon at Allianz Stadium Twickenham

Will Joseph scored five tries on his first England appearance since 2022 as Steve Borthwick's side destroyed Japan 78-15 in Saturday's Nations Championship.

Joseph (five), Freddie Steward, Ellis Genge, Cadan Murley, Ben Earl, George Martin, Ben Curry, Marcus Smith and Greg Fisilau each scored tries on a day when Japan appeared alarmingly inferior to the hosts, copping a 20-minute red card to lock Harry Hockings after just a minute of play.

Indeed, England's points total would even have been 16 greater had eight conversions not been missed off the kicking tee - George Ford missing six, Henry Slade two.

England - Tries: Joseph (1,10,20,25,56), Steward (15), Genge (18), Murley (29), Earl (40), Martin (45), Curry (64), Smith (68), Fisilau (73). Cons: Ford (15,19,41), Slade (57,69). Pens: Ford (8).

Japan - Tries: Dearns (37), Helu (48). Cons: Saito (38). Pens: Saito (14).

Japan scored tries through lock Warner Dearns and replacement prop Opeti Helu, but it was a rather sombre return for former England head coach Eddie Jones to Twickenham, with his side falling well short of professional standards.

The Test could hardly have started worse for Japan: Joseph sprinting and powering clear down the right in acres of space to score inside a minute, and the TMO bringing Hockings' high tackle on Genge to the referee's attention before Ford even took the conversion.

That left Japan down to 14, and by the sixth minute news came from the bunker Hockings' yellow had been upgraded to a 20-minute red.

Two minutes later, England captain Maro Itoje somewhat bizarrely chose to kick for three points off the kicking tee after a scrum penalty, but Joseph soon had his second, collecting a clever Steward grubber-kick angled towards the corner.

Naoto Saito kicked over a 40-metre penalty for Japan to get onto the board, but England had their third try in the 15th minute: Steward finishing after Martin had bulldozed his way forward.

Within moments, Genge stormed over for England's fourth as England cut through at will and he handed off a succession of Japanese defenders, with Joseph completing his hat-trick inside 20 minutes seconds later, flying over in the corner again.

The Gloucester wing continued to show off his pace and power, bamboozling Japan to score his fourth in the 24th minute, before opposite wing Murley slid over for a try in the corner for England's seventh inside half an hour.

With Japan missing out on a try when tighthead Shuhei Takeuchi was held up, the visitors were next to score in any case as Dearns finished strongly from close range.

England had the final say of the first period, however, as a dominant rolling maul saw Earl get in on the scoring act for a half-time score of 49-7.

Into the second half, Ford produced a stunning 50:22 to earn England a five-metre lineout chance - one which they always looked likely to score from, and duly did through Martin.

Japan lock Michael Stolberg then made a break up the middle of the pitch from deep and was caught by Henry Pollock, but England's Luke Cowan-Dickie was sin-binned for playing the ball while offside after the line-break.

It mattered little as Japan overthrew their five-metre lineout, and Joseph soon remarkably had his fifth try of the Test after plucking an intercept and running clear.

When Curry and Smith went over for England's 11th and 12th tries off lineout attacks, England's home support barely cheered, such was the disparity between the two sides.

Replacement back-row Fisilau was then awarded England's 13th try with seven minutes left, despite appearing to be held up, completing the scoring.

'Speechless' Joseph: A very special day for me

England wing and player of the match Will Joseph told ITV:

"Today was, personally, a very special day. I loved every minute of that.

"I loved the way the team moved the ball today. It was a joy to be part of. I'm speechless - it was a pretty perfect day.

"There were a few changes, and it was a short turnaround, but we got together really quickly. The performance we put in today just shows how hard we've been working behind the scenes.

"I'm going to enjoy today, then we'll be in Sunday and get our heads round the All Blacks. That's another challenge I'm looking forward to being part of - if selected!"

'Proud' Itoje: I don't even know how many tries Joseph scored!

"Japan are a tricky team who gave Wales problems last week but we dealt with those problems.

"I'm super proud of our guys - the guys who came in, Archie [McParland] making his debut, Will making his second cap - I don't even know how many tries he scored!

For England, they next face New Zealand in their third Nations Championship Test of the autumn at Allianz Stadium Twickenham on Saturday, November 21 (2.10pm kick-off).

England's Nations Championship fixtures and results

Japan travel to face Scotland at Murrayfield in Edinburgh for their next Test, also on Saturday November 21 (2.10pm kick-off).

articles.title: Nations Championship - Wales 35-28 New Zealand: Hosts display immense defence to pull off first win vs All Blacks since 1953
articles.summary: Wales pulled off one of rugby's biggest shocks of recent times as immense defence saw them to a 35-28 Nations Championship victory over New Zealand - a first against the All Blacks since 1953.
articles.body:
Tomos Williams, Dewi Lake, Archie Griffin, Eddie James, Louis Rees-Zammit score tries as Wales stun New Zealand with first win over All Blacks since 1953 in Saturday's Nations Championship; All Blacks narrowed to within seven in second half, but wave after wave of attack repelled by hosts

Wales pulled off one of rugby's biggest shocks of recent times as immense defence saw them to a 35-28 Nations Championship victory over New Zealand - a first against the All Blacks since 1953.

Wales' victory was built on the foundation of some of their best 40 minutes of rugby for some time in the first half, leading 14-0 and 21-7 after tries from scrum-half Tomos Williams, hooker Dewi Lake and tighthead Archie Griffin.

A decision to keep playing deep in the first half instead of kicking out proved costly, though, allowing New Zealand to level the contest by the break via tries from scrum-half Cortez Ratima, No 8 Wallace Sititi and wing Fehi Fineanganofo - the last score coming three minutes into dead time at the end of the first half.

Yet, Wales emerged and flew into a big lead again at the start of the second half, scoring converted tries through centre Eddie James and wing Louis Rees-Zammit for a 35-21 advantage.

Peter Lakai quickly narrowed the deficit to seven with an All Blacks try, and the remainder of the contest was played out almost exclusively inside the Wales 22, only for the home side to repel wave after wave of attack, holding New Zealand up three times in-goal.

Wales - Tries: Williams (2), Lake (6), Griffin (24), James (44), Rees-Zammit (48). Cons: Costelow (3,7,25,45,49).

New Zealand - Tries: Ratima (10), Sititi (31), Fineanganofo (43), Lakai (53). Cons: Mo'unga (10,32,44,54).

Wales made an astonishing start to the contest, creating space down the right for Rees-Zammit to chip ahead and Williams to score a try off a kind bounce after just 90 seconds.

Into the sixth minute, Wales had a second try as their early pressure and exuberance gave way to a strong finish from captain Lake, scoring after a rolling maul had made decent ground in the New Zealand 22.

Staring at a 14-0 scoreline, New Zealand quickly woke up to score their opening try in the 10th minute: scrum-half Ratima breaking off a maul to dart over past poor Welsh defence.

Yet, Wales came strong again as centre Max Llewellyn knocked on a chance he should have scored in the 23rd minute, with the hosts maintaining their composure to grab a third through impressive prop Griffin from close range.

Past the half-hour mark, New Zealand hit back again as back-row Sititi fought his way over after another driving maul in the Wales 22.

As the half drew to a close, Wales twice had opportunities to kick the ball off and bring things to the break, but instead played on in search of further points.

It proved a major error when the All Blacks attacked from deep, and kept making ground and offloading until wing Fineanganofo finished by the posts.

When Richie Mo'unga converted, the score was level at 21-21 at half-time, with Wales no doubt disappointed not to be in the lead after their impressive first half.

The home side came out in the second half undeterred, however, building through Rees-Zammit down the right again, and eventually creating space for James to finish in the left corner.

Sam Costelow converted brilliantly for a 28-21 lead, and moments later the Welsh had a fifth try through Rees-Zammit - turning down a kickable penalty in favour of a five-metre lineout, and executing perfectly off the set-piece to score.

With a lead of 35-21, James then made a remarkable tackle on Anton Lienert-Brown to save a try, but it proved little more than a delay of the inevitable as Lakai dived to ground on the line, narrowing the gap to seven points just five minutes after Wales' latest try.

On the hour mark, Sititi was held up over the try-line by Gareth Thomas when a try looked easier to score, before 21 phases of All Blacks attack were ended by a superb Jac Morgan breakdown turnover.

With 15 minutes to play, James Botham held up Asafo Aumua to deny the All Blacks again, before Wales somehow denied the visitors once more after a lengthy stanza of attack gave way to another call of held-up.

The All Blacks kept coming, but Wales' defence proved inspired to get them over the line for a famous, and wholly unexpected, victory.

Wales back row James Botham, speaking on ITV:

"I can't even describe the emotions. 1953 was the last time we beat the All Blacks.

"It's come from belief. The crowd was behind us - I just want to thank the energy and the noise behind us - you were unbelievable.

"It would be rude not to have a celebration tonight!"

Former Wales international Sam Warburton, speaking on ITV:

"To every fan, the 55,000 who put their hands in their pockets to still watch Wales, this will be so sweet.

"We forget what this playing group has gone through. From Grand Slam champions to one of the longest losing streaks for a tier one nation - they were in the pits.

"Proud to be Welsh on a day like today - those players were magnificent."

For Wales, they next face Australia in their third Nations Championship Test of the autumn at the Principality Stadium in Cardiff on Saturday, November 21 (8.10pm kick-off).

New Zealand travel to face England at Allianz Stadium Twickenham for their next Test, also on Saturday, November 21 (2.10pm kick-off).

articles.title: Wales 35-28 New Zealand: Wales beat All Blacks for first time since 1953
articles.summary: Wales celebrate a first victory against New Zealand since 1953 with a brilliant 35-28 win to spark astonishing scenes in Cardiff.
articles.body:
Tries: T Williams, Lake, Griffin, James, Rees-Zammit Cons: Costelow 5

Tries: Ratima, Sititi, Fineanganofo, Lakai Cons: Mo'unga 4.

Wales celebrated a first victory against New Zealand in 73 years with a brilliant performance to spark astonishing scenes in Cardiff.

Steve Tandy's unfancied side lifted a nation as they broke a 34-match losing sequence against the All Blacks that stretched back to 1953.

In a nine-try Nations Championship thriller at the Principality Stadium, Wales led 14-0, 21-7 and 35-21 before they held off New Zealand with a wonderful defensive display in the final quarter, led by flankers James Botham and Jac Morgan and lock Dafydd Jenkins.

The home side produced a stunning start with tries from inspirational scrum-half Tomos Williams and captain Dewi Lake inside the first six minutes.

Prop Archie Griffin also added a first-half try, but New Zealand responded with scores from scrum-half Cortez Ratima, number eight Wallace Sititi and wing Fehi Fineanganofo to level the score 21-21 at half-time.

Wales centre Eddie James and wing Louis Rees-Zammit scored early second-half tries before New Zealand flanker Peter Lakai pulled one back.

The remarkable Wales defence followed as they held up the All Blacks three times over the line to stop New Zealand scoring, to evoke wild celebrations.

Wales believed they could create history - Lake

All Blacks ran into a Welsh brick wall - Barrett

Wales had won the first three games in this fixture in 1905, 1935 and 1953 but have had to wait more than seven decades for the next.

In 1953 the New Zealand dollar did not exist, Cardiff was not the capital city of Wales and tries were only worth three points.

Sections of the New Zealand media had belittled Welsh rugby before the game, while some bookmakers offered odds of 20-1 for a Wales victory.

Legends such as Sir Gareth Edwards, Alun Wyn Jones, Shane Williams, JPR Williams, Barry John and Phil Bennett had never enjoyed success against New Zealand in a Welsh jersey.

Now Tandy's class of 2026 have written their own chapter in Welsh rugby's history.

The 55,152 was the lowest crowd in the 14 matches between Wales and New Zealand at the Principality Stadium. The fans who stayed away will regret it because it was a day to say "I was there".

Welsh rugby has been in the doldrums for so long, on and off the field, but will hope this famous victory can help galvanise the nation.

This was one of the finest performances in Welsh rugby history and a world apart from the display in the 28-21 win against Japan last weekend.

New Zealand might regret failing to take advantage of France's victory against South Africa on Friday night but they still leapfrog the Springboks to top the southern section with one weekend of regular matches remaining.

Fast start for Wales as hosts dare to dream

Wales made four changes to the side that beat Japan, with Taine Basham making his first Test start in four years by replacing injured number eight Aaron Wainwright.

Leicester wing Gabriel Hamer-Webb was preferred to Josh Adams, who scored two tries against Japan, while lock Adam Beard and flanker Botham came in for Ben Carter and Alex Mann.

New Zealand made eight starting swaps from the team that beat Scotland 43-21 , with full-back Beauden Barrett handed the Test captaincy for the first time in his 149th international.

New Zealand's haka was the usual piece of theatre as the All Blacks were lit up by a spotlight and Wales in red.

The hosts reacted quickest from the start with prop Nicky Smith winning a turnover before an excellent long pass from Williams released Rees-Zammit.

The wing chipped ahead and Williams, who New Zealand coach Dave Rennie had highlighted as a pre-match dangerman, pounced for the try.

Wales followed this up with a well-worked forward move and captain Lake latched onto a flat Williams pass to crash over.

It was the first time Wales had led New Zealand by 14 points and the home crowd began to dream.

New Zealand bounce back to level the scores

New Zealand seemed shell-shocked but regathered themselves, and Ratima strolled over for an easy try from an attacking line-out.

Rennie stated before the match they needed to eliminate the threat of Morgan at the breakdown, but they failed to do that when the Wales flanker forced a turnover penalty.

This provided the platform for New Zealand-born Wales full-back Blair Murray to release Rees-Zammit, with only good defensive work by Beauden Barrett preventing a try.

New Zealand's defence kept Wales at bay with some important turnovers before a breathless period of play followed with both sides throwing wild passes.

Once matters had settled down, New Zealand made an unusual decision to go for a scrum in the Wales 22 after being given a penalty. This backfired when the visitors were penalised and it provided the hosts with fresh momentum.

The Wales line-out, which broke down against Japan with six throws going astray, was excellent in the opening quarter and provided the foundation for the third try.

After centre Max Llewellyn was initially denied under the All Blacks' posts, prop Griffin popped up for his second try in two weeks.

New Zealand learned from their earlier error by going for an attacking line-out rather than a scrum and Sititi, who was player of the match in this fixture 12 months ago, eventually dived over.

The All Blacks demonstrated their doggedness at the breakdown by forcing two penalties, while the home line-out began to creak with two overthrows.

New Zealand began to grind away and wing Fineanganofo flopped over with Mo'unga's conversion levelling the scores at half-time.

Wales buck history trend to celebrate victory

This was the time we assumed the script would follow the familiar tale of New Zealand pulling away. Wales had other ideas.

The hosts began the second half in the same fashion as the first, with scrum-half Williams again the architect as his long pass allowed James to crash over.

Morgan again tormented New Zealand to force another turnover penalty. Wales decided to go for the try and the decision was justified.

Williams' long pass allowed Rees-Zammit to cross for the fifth try which is the highest amount scored by Wales against New Zealand.

Two tries inside the first six minutes in the first half for Wales. A pair of scores inside eight minutes in the second.

New Zealand again regrouped, with flanker Lakai burrowing over as the All Blacks came within seven points.

Lakai almost inspired a fifth Kiwi try with a fine break but replacement prop Gareth Thomas had other ideas by expertly holding up Sititi over the Wales line, before Botham repeated the feat on hooker Asafo Aumua.

Replacement Wales eight Taine Plumtree gained two important turnovers before Tandy decided to take off his half-backs Williams and Costelow, with Ospreys duo Dan Edwards and Reuben Morgan-Williams tasked to see out the final 16 minutes.

Edwards and Morgan combined to hold up New Zealand for a third time over the line but the All Blacks onslaught kept coming.

Wales dug deep once more, tapping reserves of strength, discipline and concentration to repel that black wave.

The final whistle delivered the win this side and nation have deserved for so long, reducing players and fans alike to tears of joy.

Wales: Murray; Rees-Zammit, E James, Llewellyn, Hamer-Webb; Costelow, Tomos Williams; N Smith, Lake (capt), Griffin, D Jenkins, Beard, Botham, Morgan Basham.

Replacements: Elias, G Thomas, D Lewis, Carter, Plumtree, Morgan-Williams, Edwards, Hennessey.

New Zealand: B Barrett (capt); Fineanganofo, Tupaea, Lienert-Brown, Moorby; Mo'unga, Ratima; Bower, Aumua, Newell, S Barrett, Lord, Segner, Lakai, Sititi.

Replacements: Bell, Numia, Tosi, Hannah, E Blackadder, Fainga'anuku, Preston, R Ioane.

Assistants referees: Nic Berry (Australia) & Luc Ramos (France)

Television match official (TMO): Tual Trainini (France)

Foul Play Review Officer (FPRO) : Leo Colgan (IRFU).

articles.title: Beauden Barrett: All Blacks could not get through Wales' brick wall
articles.summary: New Zealand captain Beauden Barrett praises Wales' brick wall defence after the All Blacks are stunned in Cardiff.
articles.body:
Beauden Barrett said it felt like New Zealand were running into a red brick wall after they became the first All Blacks side to lose to Wales since 1953.

Steve Tandy's men created history with a 35-28 victory at Principality Stadium thanks to a stirring defensive effort.

Wales scored five tries - a national record against New Zealand - but it was their effort without the ball that ended a 34-game losing streak against the All Blacks.

The home side made 346 tackles, with lock Dafydd Jenkins topping the chart with 38, and held the New Zealanders up over the line three times in the second half to protect their seven-point lead.

"It felt like a brick wall at times, so you have to give them credit," said full-back Barrett, who captained New Zealand in a Test for the first time.

"You give opportunities for the crowd to come into the game, and we are well aware of that when we come here.

"That's why it's one of the best places to play rugby - it feels like you are playing 16 or 17."

Magnificent Wales end 73-year New Zealand hoodoo

Wales believed they could create history - Lake

As it happened: Wales claim first win over New Zealand since 1953

Dave Rennie claimed an unwanted piece of history as the first All Blacks coach to lose to Wales in 73 years.

The former Glasgow boss admitted New Zealand "certainly got out-passioned" but had no regrets about his selection.

The All Blacks made eight changes to their starting line-up between their win against Scotland and their trip to England in the final Nations Championship group game.

"We had a good enough side on the field to win, and if you look at the stats, we had plenty of opportunities and the guys created a lot of chances," said Rennie.

"We just weren't clinical enough, and they were very good defensively.

"I have no regret around the side that we picked, as I've talked about previously, there is really good competition for places.

"There's not a lot between certain positions."

Beaten All Blacks climb above Springboks

New Zealand still inched above South Africa, who lost a thriller in France on Friday, into top spot in the southern hemisphere table.

If the All Blacks win with a bonus point at Twickenham on Saturday (14:10 GMT), they will secure top spot before the Springboks' game in Ireland (20:10 GMT).

"It hurts, but you've got to take it on the chin," said Rennie, who took over from Scott Robertson at the start of the year.

"We weren't good enough; Wales were passionate and every time they kept us out, they grew and became harder to break down.

"We've got to be better, we expect a lot more of ourselves, and I need to see a response at Twickenham."

articles.title: Wales 35-28 New Zealand: Captain Dewi Lake believed in All Blacks history
articles.summary: Captain Dewi Lake says he always believed Wales could defeat New Zealand and end the 73-year hoodoo against the All Blacks.
articles.body:
Captain Dewi Lake says he always believed Wales could defeat New Zealand and end the 73-year hoodoo against the All Blacks.

Wales never trailed in the 35-28 victory as they produced a magnificent display to beat New Zealand for the first time since 1953.

Wales had lost the previous 34 matches in the fixture and had odds of 20-1 with the bookmakers before this game.

But Lake says the group thought they could win against a New Zealand team ranked second in the world and would have gone top if they had beaten Wales.

"Of course we did," said Lake. "Sometimes we sit in front of the media and say we can beat them and it's probably a passing comment for some media outlets or people at home.

"It's not for us. We work hard, we have tough conversations, not only players, but coaches and staff.

"There is much hard work that goes on for this group to grow and succeed.

"For it to finally come to fruition and see it on the field makes me so proud."

Lake's sentiments were echoed by head coach Tandy, who said he felt emotional after the win.

"You could see what it means for the the players, nation and supporters," said Tandy.

"It's incredible. We've been wanting some positivity and the players delivered that.

"The overriding emotion is pride for the playing group, the staff and I'm just glad for everyone who represents Wales.

"You always have belief. History tells you something different but I believe in the group.

"They are a special group of people and I can't wait to come in every Monday to work with them."

Nations Championship: Wales end 73-year wait to beat New Zealand - reaction

Magnificent Wales end 73-year New Zealand hoodoo

All Blacks ran into a Welsh brick wall - Barrett

Lake's half-time team talk galvanises Wales

Wales led 14-0 and 21-7 in the first half before the All Blacks levelled the score at half-time.

That is when New Zealand have traditionally gone away to secure victory, as they did 12 months ago in a 52-26 success, but there was no repeat this time.

"I did love it at half-time with the playing group, listening to them talk to each other," said Tandy.

"The way the skipper spoken about around what's coming from the next 40 minutes was outstanding."

Lake added: "I won't tell you exactly what I said because I think that's a privilege that the group that we're in the room should keep.

"But it was more or less a flashback to 12 months ago when we were in a similar position at half-time.

"We were not quite in the lead or drawing, but there or thereabouts and it was just a reminder of that feeling for us."

Wales responded with two more tries before New Zealand brought back the deficit to within seven points.

What followed was a defensive effort rarely seen by Wales in recent years with Gareth Thomas, James Botham, Jac Morgan and Dan Edwards involved in holding up New Zealand over the home line on three occasions, while there were also two vital turnovers from replacement Taine Plumtree.

The home side made 346 tackles, with lock Dafydd Jenkins topping the chart with 38 and flankers Morgan and Botham not far behind.

The work of Tandy and defensive coaching duo Peter Murchie and Dan Lydiate was rewarded with heart and skill.

"The players were brave but also phenomenal and showed great physicality," said Tandy.

"New Zealand threw everything at us but the boys got what they deserved and in big games you have to hang on."

Final whistle mayhem but attention turns towards Australia

There might have been only 55,152 in the ground, which was the lowest attendance for a Wales and New Zealand fixture at the Principality Stadium, but they roared the home side onto a famous victory.

Lake summed up the events at the final whistle as he was on the sidelines after being replaced.

"It was almost like you were blocked out things, said Lake.

"You heard the noise, but it was like background noise. I think I stopped watching with a minute and 20 seconds left and just waited for the whistle, which I have done before, but this one was different.

"To celebrate with the boys that you work hard with every day, and the coaches that come in and make you better, is an amazing feeling.

Lock Jenkins stated before the game he was asking for Monday off if Wales beat New Zealand, with Tandy's side facing Australia in Cardiff next Saturday.

"We've got to savour moments, because history tells you this doesn't happen very often, and we need to make make sure we enjoy this," said Tandy.

"I'm sure every rugby club out there is going to be celebrating tonight but it's making sure when we come in, maybe Monday afternoon or Tuesday morning, if Daf gets his way, that we're ready to work.

"Because Australia will be a different test."

That can wait as Wales reflect on halting New Zealand's seven decades of dominance over them.

articles.title: England 78-15 Japan: Will Joseph scores five as hosts rout Brave Blossoms
articles.summary: Will Joseph marked his comeback after four years out the Test game with a record-equalling five tries as England tore through Japan.
articles.body:
Tries: Joseph 5, Steward, Genge, Murley, Earl, Martin, B Curry, M Smith, Fisilau Cons: Ford 4, Slade Pen: Ford

Tries: Dearns, Helu Con: Saito Pen: Saito

Will Joseph marked his comeback after four years out the Test game with a record-equalling five tries as England tore through Japan and set their sights on New Zealand next weekend.

A teenage Joseph made his debut as a late replacement in a game against Australia four years ago.

Since then he has endured his boyhood club London Irish going bust, an underwhelming spell at Harlequins and the loss of hearing in his left ear after an auto-immune reaction.

But his superb early season form for Gloucester has thrust him back into the international picture and he took his opportunity superbly, showing work-rate and intelligence as well as raw top-end speed.

Four other players - Douglas Lambert, Rory Underwood, Josh Lewsey and Henry Arundell - have scored five tries in a single match for England.

Japan were vastly over-matched, unable to rev up the ball movement and quickfire rucks that have made them a threat to the game's major powers in the past.

With the outcome clear as England raced out to a 32-3 lead inside 20 minutes, the focus sharpened on a number of individuals attempting to press their case alongside Joseph.

Centre Max Ojomoh, making his first appearance since an excellent performance against Argentina 12 months ago, was smart and sharp in midfield.

The Bath man burst into a pocket of space to help set up Joseph's second and his slick hands opened up a corridor of space for his team-mate's gleefully acrobatic fourth as Japan were buried beneath an avalanche of points.

Henry Pollock, afforded only his second start in his eye-catching England career, carried gamely but didn't have the impact he has shown so often off the bench.

Replacement Greg Fisilau's pair of wince-inducing hits and burrowing try added more intrigue to the back-row equation.

And while George Ford sewed together England's backline neatly enough, his failure to convert more of England's early tries won't help his hopes of regaining the 10 shirt on a more permanent basis.

Northampton scrum-half Archie McParland made his debut as a replacement, but a host of front-line names will return next Saturday as England attempt to take down an All Blacks side smarting from defeat by Wales.

'An al'An almost perfect day' - reaction after Joseph scores five tries in thumping win over Japan

Joseph fills Feyi-Waboso vacancy with aplomb

England have targeted fast starts this autumn and they tore into Japan with relish, launching into a pummelling that only let up long after victory was secure.

Joseph, tasked with bringing the pace and power lost with Immanuel Feyi-Waboso's injury, delivered almost immediately.

Feyi-Waboso had a second-minute try chalked off by the Television Match Official in last weekend's win over Australia and when referee Damian Schneider went upstairs after Joseph crossed in similar swift fashion, it looked ominous for the Gloucester man.

There was nothing wrong in England's build-up before he scorched Riku Kitahara and Warner Dearns for the score. Indeed, there was a lot right for the hosts with Pollock making yards and Ojomoh's slick mis-pass opening up space.

Instead Japan second row Harry Hockings had caught Ellis Genge with a shoulder to the head.

Hockings, upright into the collision, was shown a 20-minute red card on review.

His team, who could not cope with England with a full complement, crumbled.

England scored another four tries in the powerplay, as Eddie Jones, who coached England for nearly seven years from 2016, looking increasingly grim-faced in the coaches box.

England's forward power was an obvious edge to exploit.

Genge splattered number eight Jack Cornelsen on a fearsome charge to the line.

Big carries from George Martin and Asher Opoku-Fordjour set up a prime platform for Freddie Steward to bowl over Kitahara for a try.

Ben Earl was at the back of a stampeding driving maul with brought up a 49-10 scoreline by the break, and Martin barged over from short range early in the second half.

Joseph snaffled an interception to grab his record-equalling fifth try, trotting in while his brother and former England centre Jonathan Joseph looked on from his pitchside role as an in-stadium presenter.

Marcus Smith was given a rare chance to run at fly-half after replacing Ford on 57 minutes.

With the game breaking up and replacements disrupting rhythm, it was hard for the Harlequin to impose much of a pattern on proceedings, but he drifted nicely outside an onrushing tackler to get on the scoresheet.

Last year's victory over New Zealand was one of the high points of head coach Steve Borthwick's regime.

England came into the autumn as underdogs for this year's rematch, but the teams' performances this weekend suggest those odds are narrowing, and perhaps flipping in the hosts' favour.

England: Steward; Joseph, Slade, Ojomoh, Murley; Ford, Van Poortvliet; Genge, Cowan-Dickie, Opoku-Fordjour, Itoje (capt), Martin, Coles, Earl, Pollock

Replacements: Dan, Iyogun, Heyes, Clark, B Curry, Fisilau, McParland, M Smith

Japan: Ueda; Ishida, Riley, Tua, Tokito; Kitahara, Saito (co-capt); Kamimori, Harada, Takeuchi, Hockings, Dearns (co-capt), Gunter, Shimokawa, Cornelsen

Replacements: Sato, Otsuka, Helu, Stolberg, Costley, Fujiwara, Komura, Lee

Assistant referees: Ben O'Keeffe (New Zealand) and Craig Evans (Wales)

TMO: Marius van der Westhuizen (South Africa)

Foul Play Review Officer: Aled Griffiths (Wales)

articles.title: Nations Championship - Wales 35-28 New Zealand: Steve Tandy hails 'phenomenal' players after historic win over All Blacks
articles.summary: Steve Tandy branded his players "phenomenal" after their historic Nations Championship win over New Zealand; Wales beat All Blacks for first time in 73 years, ending run of 34 successive defeats
articles.body:
It was the first time since 1953 that Wales could celebrate beating the All Blacks, ending a run of 34 successive defeats in one of world rugby's historically most one-sided fixtures.

On three separate occasions Wales led by 14 points, and for the first time they scored five tries against New Zealand, but ultimately it was heroic defensive work that denied the visitors.

"I feel pride for the players, and to see what it means to the supporters," head coach Tandy said. "We have been wanting some positivity, and I think the players delivered that today.

"We knew it was going to be brutal on both sides of the ball, and I thought the intent from minute one was exceptional.

"You always have belief. They are a special group of people, and there will be lots of bumps along the road, but the boys can be super-proud today.

"The players were phenomenal. New Zealand threw everything at us, and it is just an amazing feeling. We have got to savour moments like this.

"This is a real good statement win for us, and we have got to enjoy it, but we have got to keep going and building performances. We have got a massive game against Australia next week."

First-half tries from Tomos Williams, Dewi Lake and Archie Griffin - all converted by Sam Costelow - put Wales in charge, although New Zealand clawed it back to 21-21 as Cortez Ratima, Wallace Sititi and Fehi Fineanganofo all touched down, with Richie Mo'unga booting three conversions.

All Blacks head coach Dave Rennie made eight changes from the side that swept past Scotland in their previous Nations Championship game, and such an approach ultimately backfired, with Eddie James and Louis Rees-Zammit adding further Wales scores that Costelow converted.

New Zealand mustered a fourth touchdown from flanker Peter Lakai, yet try as they might, there was no further way over the Wales line as tackle after tackle kept them out.

Wales captain Dewi Lake added: "To put on the field what we did today, to make history, is tough to put into words, but it is nothing this group doesn't deserve for the work they have put in.

"Sometimes we sit in front of the media and say we can beat them, and it is probably a passing comment for some people at home, but it's not for us. You wouldn't believe the work that goes on for this group to go out and succeed.

"The boys dug in hard, a lot of defensive sets, three or four hold-ups over the line. I think I stopped watching with one minute, 20 seconds left and just waited for the whistle! It is an amazing feeling."

Barrett: Wales defence felt like brick wall

Three Wales players - Dafydd Jenkins, Jac Morgan and James Botham - each made more than 30 tackles, and New Zealand skipper Beauden Barrett conceded how tough it had been to break Wales down in the second half.

"It is a tough one to take, particularly when we were building a lot of pressure but couldn't convert into points," Barrett said.

"It felt like a brick wall at times, so you have to give Wales credit. We were a little bit indecisive, we had three hold-ups over the line, and we have got be better at converting those opportunities."

All Blacks head coach Dave Rennie, meanwhile, said: "We are massively disappointed. We started both halves poorly and conceded 14 points quickly. We had plenty of territory, and we need to be a lot better than that.

"Credit to Wales. They were really clinical when they got their chances, and they defended for massive amounts and were the better side.

"We got a bit one-dimensional, and that's decision-making under pressure. They ran hard on to the ball, and we struggled to slow it down."

For Wales, they next face Australia in their third Nations Championship Test of the autumn at the Principality Stadium in Cardiff on Saturday, November 21 (8.10pm kick-off).

New Zealand travel to face England at Allianz Stadium Twickenham for their next Test, also on Saturday, November 21 (2.10pm kick-off).
